blocks.x: Glycogen is the body's rapid-access storage form of glucose — a large, highly branched polymer built entirely from glucose units. When blood sugar is plentiful, cells lock glucose away as glycogen; when it's needed, they break it back down. It's stored mainly in the liver and skeletal muscle, and all of its synthesis and breakdown happens in the cytosol.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a pantry stocked with easy-to-grab snacks

blocks.x: Think of fat as the deep-freezer in the garage: huge capacity, but slow to get to. Glycogen is the kitchen pantry — much smaller, but right there when you need a quick bite. The body keeps glucose in this pantry so it can grab energy fast, without waiting on the slow freezer. The pantry fills when you've just eaten and empties between meals or during exercise.

Structurally, glucose units are joined in long chains by α-1,4 glycosidic bonds, with α-1,6 branch points creating a branch roughly every 8–10 residues. Every glycogen molecule is built on a core protein called glycogenin, giving it one reducing end (anchored to glycogenin) and many non-reducing ends — the branch tips where glucose is added and removed.

The heavy branching isn't decoration — it's speed. Every branch tip (a non-reducing end) is a place where enzymes can add or pull off glucose. Hundreds of tips mean hundreds of workers can act on one molecule at once, so glycogen can be built up or torn down very fast. It also keeps the molecule compact and soluble.

sections.title: Two storage sites, two completely different jobs

blocks.x: Liver and muscle both store glycogen, but for opposite reasons. The liver is an altruist — it stores glucose to release into the blood for the whole body. Muscle is selfish — it hoards glucose purely for its own contraction.

c: Maintain blood glucose for the whole body
More total (~250–400 g — muscle mass is large)
Yes — can release free glucose to blood

blocks.title: The single most important difference — glucose-6-phosphatase

blocks.x: Only the liver has the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase. This one enzyme is why liver glycogen can raise your blood sugar but muscle glycogen can't. Muscle keeps its glucose trapped as glucose-6-phosphate (which is charged and can't cross the membrane) and burns it on-site. Remember this — it explains a huge amount of glycogen physiology and disease.

sections.title: Building glycogen up, glucose by glucose

blocks.x: Glycogenesis is how cells store incoming glucose. The key idea: before a glucose can be added, it must first be activated into a special high-energy donor form, UDP-glucose.

blocks.cap: Glucose-6-P → glucose-1-P → activated UDP-glucose → added to the chain → branched.

blocks.x: Phosphoglucomutase shifts the phosphate to make glucose-1-phosphate. (This step is reversible and shared with breakdown.)
UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase combines glucose-1-P with UTP to form UDP-glucose — the activated glucose donor. This is the committed, energy-investing step of synthesis.
Glycogen synthase — the key regulated enzyme — attaches the glucose to a growing chain via an α-1,4 bond. It can only extend an existing chain; it can't start one.
Branching enzyme picks up a block of ~6–7 glucose units and re-attaches it as a new α-1,6 branch (the donor chain must be ≥11 units, and branches sit ≥4 units apart).

Glycogen synthase is like a bricklayer who can extend a wall but can't lay the very first brick on bare ground. So there's a special self-starting protein, glycogenin, that acts as the primer: it attaches the first few glucose units to itself (self-glucosylation), creating the short starter chain that glycogen synthase then builds on. Every glycogen molecule has a glycogenin core.

sections.title: Tearing glycogen down when glucose is needed

blocks.x: Glycogenolysis releases glucose from storage. The workhorse enzyme, glycogen phosphorylase, doesn't use water to cut the bonds — it uses inorganic phosphate, a trick called phosphorolysis.

Glycogen phosphorylase snips glucose units off the non-reducing ends one at a time, releasing glucose-1-phosphate. It's the rate-limiting enzyme of breakdown. But it stalls 4 units away from a branch point, leaving a stub called a limit dextrin.

The debranching enzyme is bifunctional: its transferase activity moves 3 of the 4 remaining glucose units onto a nearby chain end, then its α-1,6-glucosidase activity snips off the final branch-point glucose as free glucose (not phosphorylated).
Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate — the same reversible enzyme used in synthesis, just running the other way.

In the liver, glucose-6-phosphatase (in the ER) strips the phosphate off, and free glucose exits via GLUT2 into the blood. Muscle lacks this enzyme, so its glucose-6-P instead feeds straight into glycolysis for the muscle's own energy.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — stripping fruit off a heavily-branched tree

blocks.x: Phosphorylase is a fast picker that strips fruit from the tips of every branch — but it can't reach the fruit right at the forks where branches split. So a second specialist (the debranching enzyme) steps in: it first relocates a small cluster of fruit to a reachable spot, then plucks off the very last piece stuck at the fork. Only then can the fast picker keep going down the main branch.

sections.title: One master switch, flipped two opposite ways

blocks.x: The body must never build and break glycogen at the same time — that would waste energy. So the two key enzymes are controlled by the same switch (phosphorylation) but in opposite directions. This is the single most important idea in glycogen regulation.

blocks.title: The see-saw — phosphorylation flips both at once

blocks.x: Picture a single see-saw. When a phosphate group is added (during fasting/stress), breakdown goes UP and synthesis goes DOWN — because phosphorylation activates phosphorylase but inactivates synthase. When the phosphate is removed (well-fed), the see-saw tips the other way. One switch, opposite effects — so the two never run at once.
The hormones work through a cascade that amplifies the signal enormously:

Glucagon (liver) or epinephrine (liver + muscle) → binds its receptor → raises cAMP → activates Protein Kinase A (PKA) → activates phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase → glycogen breakdown. Each step multiplies the signal, so a tiny hormone pulse triggers a massive glucose release.
Insulin lowers cAMP and activates protein phosphatase-1 (PP1), which removes the phosphates: synthase switches on, phosphorylase switches off — so glucose gets stored.

Glucose-6-phosphate allosterically activates synthase and inhibits phosphorylase (plenty of glucose around → store it). In muscle, AMP (low energy) activates phosphorylase, and a rise in Ca²⁺ during contraction activates phosphorylase kinase directly — linking breakdown to the very act of contracting.

sections.title: What happens when an enzyme is missing?

blocks.x: <term d="Inherited disorders in which a defective enzyme of glycogen metabolism causes abnormal amounts or structure of glycogen to accumulate, damaging affected organs.">Glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)</term> are inherited defects in the enzymes above. Each one maps neatly onto the pathway — knowing the enzyme tells you the organ affected and the symptoms.

c: Glycogen builds up in lysosomes; heart affected
Enlarged liver and mild fasting hypoglycaemia — a milder, liver-only picture

blocks.title: McArdle vs Hers — the same enzyme, two different organs

blocks.x: Both are a fault in glycogen phosphorylase, so the difference is purely which version is affected. McArdle (V) hits the muscle enzyme — so the problem shows up during exercise: cramps, weakness, and no rise in blood lactate on exertion. Hers (VI) hits the liver enzyme — so the problem shows up during fasting: an enlarged liver and mild low blood sugar, but exercise is fine. Muscle = movement problem; liver = blood-sugar problem.

blocks.title: Two that are easy to mix up — Von Gierke vs McArdle

blocks.x: Von Gierke (I) is a liver problem: without glucose-6-phosphatase, the liver can't release glucose, so blood sugar crashes during fasting. McArdle (V) is a muscle problem: without muscle phosphorylase, muscle can't tap its own glycogen, so it cramps and tires quickly during exercise — but blood sugar is fine because the liver is untouched. Match the enzyme's location to the symptom and these become straightforward.

items: Glycogen is a branched glucose polymer (α-1,4 chains, α-1,6 branches every 8–10 units) built on a glycogenin core, stored in liver and muscle; all metabolism is cytosolic.
Liver glycogen serves blood glucose for the whole body; muscle glycogen fuels only itself. Only liver has glucose-6-phosphatase to release free glucose.
Glycogenesis: glucose-6-P → glucose-1-P → UDP-glucose (activated donor) → glycogen synthase adds α-1,4 units → branching enzyme adds α-1,6 branches. Glycogenin primes new chains.
Glycogenolysis: phosphorylase releases glucose-1-P by phosphorolysis (stalls 4 from a branch = limit dextrin) → bifunctional debranching enzyme clears the branch → phosphoglucomutase → glucose-6-P.

Regulation: phosphorylation activates phosphorylase ("a") but inactivates synthase — one switch, opposite effects. Glucagon/epinephrine → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylase kinase → breakdown. Insulin & PP1 reverse it; G6P, AMP, Ca²⁺ fine-tune it.
Storage diseases: Von Gierke (I, glucose-6-phosphatase), Pompe (II, lysosomal glucosidase), Cori (III, debrancher), Andersen (IV, brancher), McArdle (V, muscle phosphorylase).

lines: "4 in a line, 6 to branch" — α-1,4 bonds make the straight chains; α-1,6 bonds make the branches.
"Liver is generous, Muscle is selfish" — only liver (with glucose-6-phosphatase) shares glucose with the blood; muscle keeps it all for itself.
"Phosphorylate to Pulverize" — phosphorylation ACTIVATES phosphorylase (breakdown) but INACTIVATES synthase. One switch, opposite effects.
"Phosphorylase stops 4 short" — it can't get within ~4 units of a branch, leaving a limit dextrin for the debrancher to clear.
"Von Gierke = liver, McArdle = muscle" — Von Gierke (I) crashes blood sugar; McArdle (V) causes exercise cramps with normal blood sugar.
Structure: α-1,4 chains + α-1,6 branches (every 8–10 units)
Core protein: glycogenin · Location: cytosol (liver & muscle)
Liver = blood glucose for body · Muscle = own use only
Liver only: glucose-6-phosphatase → free glucose to blood
Insulin + PP1 → storage · G6P activates synthase, inhibits phosphorylase
III Cori = debrancher · IV Andersen = brancher

items.d: Glucose-6-P ↔ Glucose-1-P. Reversible; shared by synthesis and breakdown.
Glucose-1-P + UTP → UDP-glucose, the activated glucose donor for synthesis.
Adds glucose via α-1,4 bonds to extend chains. Rate-limiting step of synthesis; needs a glycogenin primer.
Moves ~6-7 glucose units to make new α-1,6 branch points (donor chain ≥11, branches ≥4 apart).
Breakdown: phosphorolysis releases glucose-1-P from chain ends. Rate-limiting; stalls ~4 units from a branch (limit dextrin).
Bifunctional: transferase moves 3 units, then α-1,6-glucosidase frees the branch-point glucose.
Glucose-6-P → free glucose released to blood via GLUT2. Muscle lacks this, so it burns glucose-6-P itself.
